claims.text: A Pt-based alloy catalyst with strain- and defect-engineered near-surface structure will exhibit enhanced HER and HOR activity relative to an unmodified Pt catalyst.
A Pt-based alloy catalyst with strain- and defect-engineered near-surface structure will exhibit enhanced durability relative to an unmodified Pt catalyst.
Controlled tensile or compressive strain can be induced at the surface of a Pt-based catalyst through tailored chemical, thermal, or mild electrochemical treatment.
Engineered defect sites can be created at the surface of a Pt-based catalyst through tailored chemical, thermal, or mild electrochemical treatment.
The proposed catalyst can operate for HER and HOR in acidic media.
The proposed catalyst can operate for HER and HOR in alkaline media.
Induced strain and surface defects alter the local electronic structure of the Pt-based catalyst.
The strain- and defect-induced electronic-structure changes shift hydrogen adsorption and desorption energies toward an optimum.
Optimizing hydrogen adsorption and desorption energies enhances HER kinetics.
Optimizing hydrogen adsorption and desorption energies enhances HOR kinetics.
The proposed surface modifications improve resistance to corrosion during potential cycling.
The proposed surface modifications reduce catalyst degradation during potential cycling.
The interface-engineered catalyst will have lower HER and HOR overpotential than an unmodified Pt catalyst.
The interface-engineered catalyst will have higher HER and HOR turnover frequency than an unmodified Pt catalyst.
The interface-engineered catalyst will retain activity for longer than an unmodified Pt catalyst.
Excessive atomic-scale modification may compromise the integrity of the catalyst.
The interface-engineering approach may not remain effective under operational conditions more extreme than those typical of standard electrolyzers.
